newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Halifax muscles into UK banking ring.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Halifax muscles into UK banking ring.

text.p: Former building society Halifax muscled its way into the ranks of Britain's heavyweight banks on Monday when it made its long-awaited, multi-billion pound stock exchange debut.
The flotation handed 7.6 million Britons shares worth an average of nearly 2,500 pounds ($4,090) and saw Halifax Plc, as it is now known, leap into third spot among Britain's publicly quoted banks.

With a market capitalisation of 18.4 billion pounds at the average auction price, Halifax easily makes the top 10 of Britain's 100 leading quoted companies, slotting in at number eight, the group's head of corporate affairs, Gary Marsh, said.
The new bank on the block has in fact sneaked in slightly ahead of banking rival Barclays Plc in terms of market capitalisation, he added.
Halifax was happy with the way the float had gone but analysts said the fundamentals did not justify the share's high price, which had been buoyed by strong institutional demand for the new stock.

Halifax's first day as a Plc, or public limited company, underlined the familiar investor health warning that share prices can fall as well as rise. Holders saw the price fall to 734.5 pence at the close, slightly above the level they would have achieved at auction.

Halifax initially topped market expectations, opening at 774.5 pence, but a falling stock market meant it closed just two pence above the level at which 23 percent of the 2.51 billion shares were auctioned on Friday to institutional investors.

Halifax's corporate broker Merrill Lynch told a telephone news briefing that 200 institutions, largely British but with some overseas interest, had successfully bid for the shares. They were joined on Monday by more institutional buyers as well as significant retail demand for the new stock.
The auction means nearly two million Britons will have cash to spend, while others have chosen to take the shares and wait to see how the Halifax performs.

At the average auction price a Halifax shareholder with the maximum share entitlement will have collected 10,116 pounds, while someone with the basic 200 share entitlement will have netted a windfall of 1,465 pounds.
"We hope our members will be delighted with the price," Halifax's Marsh told Reuters. "We are pleased to be able to cement our relationship with them."
But analysts said shareholders could see their shares fall in value after their impressive debut.

Merrill Lynch said Halifax was trading at a premium because of its short-term scarcity and the success of its pre-flotation roadshow, adding it would be interesting to see the extent of retail selling in the shares.

"Our analysis suggests that 600-650 pence is about where it should be, based on its fundamental prospects vis-a-vis other shares in the UK fundamental sector," John Leonard, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers, told Reuters.
"Halifax may be a great company but it is a rich share," said Leonard, who rates the stock a hold.
The cash-rich Halifax is widely predicted to give major banks National Westminster Bank Plc, Lloyds TSB, Midland and Barclays a run for their money.

Marsh declined to comment when asked whether Halifax, which has around 20 million customers and more than three billion pounds in cash, would use its new-found flexibility as a public company to make a quick acquisition.
But he repeated that Halifax would consider going on the acquisition trail. "That is one of the options we are looking at," he said.
John Tyce, banking analyst at Societe Generale, said Halifax was likely to look at further buys in the life insurance and pensions market and unsecured personal credit.
"They've already made a move on Clerical and Medical, the life insurance and pensions operator, and I think there may be further acquisitions in that area," Tyce said.

Halifax's strong franchise in the mortgage market, where it is the largest lender in Britain, and which generates around 85 percent of its profit, would also be useful in building up non-mortgage credit business, he added.

The flotation of the 144-year-old Halifax follows last month's float of the Alliance & Leicester Plc, which also ditched its mutual status, where it was owned by its members, in favour of becoming a public limited company.
Halifax says it is prepared for the trials and tribulations of life as a stock market giant.

"We are pleased we have got the reception we have as a quoted company but this is by no means the end of it for the Halifax. It's the end of one chapter but the beginning of a new one," said Halifax's Marsh.
